summary: Applies the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (GTSM) to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP). Checking a packet's TTL or hop limit shows whether it came from a node on a directly connected link, which protects a router's control plane from CPU-exhaustion attacks. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Label distribution runs between routers that should be directly connected, but nothing in the protocol stopped a message from further away. This RFC makes the two ends check the TTL of the packets, which is only 255 if the packet came straight from the neighbour's interface, and it agrees this automatically during the hello exchange.

questions: how to secure ldp with gtsm
what is the generalized ttl security mechanism
what is the ldp g flag
subtitle: Using the packet's TTL to prove that an LDP message came from the router next door.

tldr.problem: A router's LDP peering session is reachable from beyond its own link, so an attacker anywhere on the path can send it forged protocol messages and burn the router's CPU.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a G flag to the Common Hello Parameters of the LDP Link Hello, so two adjacent routers can discover each other's support for the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism and then require arriving session packets to have a TTL of 255.
tldr.outcome: The protection is negotiated by default, without configuration, and it keeps working with routers that do not know the flag, which simply means no protection for that peering.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: IPv4 routing, single-hop LDP peering sessions

today: RFC 6720 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7552, which updates LDP for IPv6. The G flag in the Common Hello Parameters TLV and the rule that session packets must arrive with a TTL of 255 remain the mechanism this document defines for LDP over IPv4.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LDP specifies two peer discovery mechanisms, a Basic one and an Extended one, both using UDP transport. The Basic Discovery mechanism is used to discover LDP peers that are directly connected at the link level, whereas the Extended Discovery mechanism is used to locate routers that are not directly connected at the link level. Once discovered, the neighbours can establish the LDP peering session over a TCP transport connection.

The Generalized TTL Security Mechanism is a mechanism based on IPv4 Time To Live or IPv6 Hop Limit value verification, so as to provide a simple and reasonably robust defence from infrastructure attacks using forged protocol packets from outside the network. GTSM can be applied to any protocol peering session that is established between routers that are adjacent, and therefore it can protect an LDP protocol peering session established using Basic Discovery.

This document specifies LDP enhancements to accommodate GTSM: the Common Hello Parameters TLV of the LDP Link Hello message, the sending and receiving procedures for that message, and the sending and receiving procedures for the LDP Initialization message.

GTSM says it should not be enabled by default in order to remain backward compatible with the unmodified protocol. This document instead specifies a built-in dynamic GTSM capability negotiation for LDP, so that the desire to use GTSM, that is its negotiation mechanics, is enabled by default without any configuration. GTSM is used as specified provided both peers on an LDP session can detect each other's support for it and agree to use it. The document uses a bit reserved in the LDP specification and therefore updates it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two routers introduce themselves to their neighbours with a UDP message, then open a TCP session for the label protocol itself. This RFC makes that introduction say, one more thing: do I support checking the TTL on the session that follows?

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
This document defines procedures for LDP using IPv4 routing but not for LDP using IPv6 routing, since the latter has GTSM built into the protocol definition.

Additionally, the GTSM for LDP specified here applies only to single-hop LDP peering sessions and not to multi-hop LDP peering sessions. Consequently, any LDP method or feature that relies on multi-hop LDP peering sessions would not work with GTSM and would require, statically or dynamically, disabling the GTSM capability. Two examples named are LDP IGP Synchronization and LDP Session Protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Two limits. It is for IPv4 routing, because the IPv6 version of the protocol already does this. And it only works between routers that are really next to each other, so features that need a peering across several routers cannot use it.

sections.title: The G Flag in the Common Hello Parameters
sections.content:
A new flag in the Common Hello Parameters TLV, named the G flag for GTSM, is defined by this document in a previously reserved bit. A router indicates that it is capable of applying GTSM procedures to the subsequent LDP peering session by setting the GTSM flag to 1.

The T flag, for Targeted Hello, and the R flag, for Request Send Targeted Hellos, are as already specified in the LDP document. The G flag has a value of 1 to specify that this router supports GTSM procedures, and a value of 0 to specify that it does not. The reserved field must be set to zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The G flag is meaningful only if the T flag is set to 0, which must be the case for Basic Discovery; otherwise the value of the G flag is ignored on receipt. Any router that does not recognize the G flag continues to ignore it, independent of the values of the T and R flags. Similarly, a router that recognizes the G flag but does not support GTSM, either because it is not implemented or because it is configured that way, would not set the G flag when sending LDP Link Hellos and would effectively ignore the G flag when receiving them.
sections.plainLanguage: One bit in the hello message says whether the sender is willing to do the TTL check. It only counts when the hello was not targeted at one particular router, which is the case for the link-wide discovery that this scheme is built on.

sections.title: Hello and Initialization Procedures
sections.content:
First, routers using LDP Basic Discovery send LDP Hello messages to the link-level multicast address 224.0.0.2, or all routers. Such messages are never forwarded beyond one hop and are recommended to have their IP TTL or hop count set to 1.

Unless configured otherwise, a router that supports GTSM procedures must set the G flag to 1 in the Common Hello Parameters TLV in the LDP Link Hello message. If such a router, configured to use GTSM, recognizes the presence of the G flag with a value of 1 in a received LDP Link Hello message, then it must enforce GTSM for LDP in the subsequent TCP and LDP peering session with the neighbour that sent the hello. If a router does not recognize the presence of the G flag, or recognizes it with a value of 0, then it must not enforce GTSM in the subsequent peering session with that neighbour. This ensures backward compatibility as well as automatic GTSM deactivation.

If a router has sent and received an LDP Link Hello with the G flag set to 1 from the directly connected neighbour, then it must enforce GTSM procedures in the forthcoming TCP transport connection with that neighbour. This means that it must check for the incoming unicast packets' TTL or hop count to be 255 for that particular LDP and TCP peering session, and decide the further processing as the GTSM document specifies. If a router sent the Link Hello with the G flag set to 1 but received one with the G flag set to 0, then it must not enforce GTSM in the forthcoming connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends say yes in their hello messages, and both then insist that every packet on the session has a TTL of exactly 255. If either end does not say yes, neither enforces the check, so an old router simply gets an unprotected session.

sections.title: Peering Scenarios and GTSM Considerations
sections.content:
The GTSM capability negotiation is enabled by default for Basic Discovery, that is with the G flag set to 1, but not for Extended Discovery, because Basic Discovery typically relates to a single-hop LDP peering session whereas Extended Discovery typically relates to a multi-hop one. GTSM protection for multi-hop LDP sessions is outside the scope of the specification. Three exceptions are worth clarifying.

In the first case, two adjacent routers forming a single-hop LDP peering session after doing an Extended Discovery, for example for pseudowire signalling, GTSM is not enabled for the LDP peering session by default. In the second case, two adjacent routers forming a multi-hop LDP peering session after doing a Basic Discovery, because of the way IP routing is set up between them, either temporarily or permanently, GTSM is actually enabled by default and enforced for the LDP peering session, and it would prohibit that session from being established. In the third case, two adjacent routers forming a single-hop LDP peering session after doing both Basic and Extended Discovery, GTSM is enabled by default for Basic Discovery and enforced on the subsequent LDP peering, and is not for Extended Discovery. However, if each router uses the same IPv4 transport address object value in both discoveries, the result is a single LDP peering session that is enabled with GTSM; otherwise GTSM is not enforced on the second peering session corresponding to the Extended Discovery.

The document allows an implementation to provide an option to statically, for example by configuration, and dynamically override the default behaviour and enable or disable GTSM on a per-peer basis, which would address all the exceptions listed above.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is simple but the world is not. If two routers discover each other over the link but their traffic actually crosses more than one hop, the TTL check will fail and the session will not form. That is why the RFC allows an operator to switch the behaviour off for a particular neighbour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document increases the security for LDP, making it more resilient to off-link attacks. The security considerations for GTSM itself are detailed in the GTSM document.

Two limitations are recorded. GTSM for LDP may not always be enforced on a single-hop LDP peering session, and LDP may still be susceptible to forged or spoofed protocol packets, if a single-hop peering session is set up using Extended Discovery. And GTSM for LDP may cause the LDP peering session not to be established, or to be torn down, if IP routing ever declares that the directly connected peer is more than one IP hop away. Cryptographic integrity is recommended as an alternate solution for detecting forged protocol packets, especially for the multi-hop case.

The GTSM specification says that protocol messages used for dynamic negotiation of GTSM support must be authenticated. LDP discovery, however, uses UDP transport and does not have an authentication mechanism. The GTSM specification further says that GTSM is not a substitute for authentication and does not secure against insider on-the-wire attacks. LDP Basic Discovery uses the link-level multicast address 224.0.0.2, whose messages are never forwarded beyond the link, and this acts as a basic protection against off-the-wire attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The check is a useful filter against attackers outside the network, but it is not authentication: the hello messages that agree to use it are not themselves protected, and someone already on the wire is not stopped. For peers that are not really adjacent, a cryptographic check is the better answer.

items.title: Basic discovery
items.text: Finds LDP peers that are directly connected at the link level, using UDP.

items.title: Extended discovery
items.text: Finds routers that are not directly connected, so the peering can span several hops.

items.title: The peering session
items.text: Once discovered, the neighbours set up the LDP session over a TCP transport connection.

items.title: GTSM
items.text: Checks the TTL or hop limit of arriving packets, which is only 255 if the packet came straight from the neighbour.

cells: Enabled and enforced, which prevents the session from forming
Single-hop session after both Basic and Extended Discovery

viz.caption: WHAT THE TTL CHECK DOES AND DOES NOT BUY

items.title: It filters off-link attacks
items.text: Forged packets that did not come from the neighbour's interface have a lower TTL and are discarded.

items.title: It is not authentication
items.text: The hello messages that agree to use GTSM are not themselves protected, and the GTSM document says GTSM does not secure against insider attacks.

items.title: It can break a session
items.text: If routing ever says the neighbour is more than one hop away, the session fails to form or is torn down.

items.title: It does not cover every peering
items.text: A single-hop session set up with Extended Discovery is not protected at all.

items.title: Use cryptography where it matters
items.text: For multi-hop peers, cryptographic integrity is the recommended alternative.
